gloss_terse: axle (of a wheeled cart or stand)
gloss_readable: Refers to the bronze axles that allowed the wheels on Solomon's temple stands to rotate. This rare technical term appears only in the description of the ten bronze stands crafted for the temple, each equipped with wheels mounted on bronze axles. The word is cognate with Aramaic, suggesting it may be a loan-word for specialized metalwork vocabulary.

senses.1: The bronze axles that supported rotating wheels on the ten movable stands in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 7:30). The Hebrew term is rare, occurring only once, and the ancient versions struggled with it—the Greek rendered it loosely as 'attachments.' The Aramaic cognate and the context of bronze-working suggest this was technical vocabulary for temple artisanry.

gloss_readable: Denotes the spreading branches of a great tree in Ezekiel's allegory of Pharaoh. The word appears uniquely in Ezekiel 31, where Egypt is pictured as a towering cedar with boughs multiplied beyond other trees. The term includes an infixed 'r' as a morphological marker, similar to Aramaic forms, pointing to its late linguistic character.

senses.1: The luxuriant boughs of the allegorical tree representing Pharaoh's Egypt (Ezekiel 31:5). Ezekiel describes how the great cedar's branches multiplied 'because of abundant water'—the image of imperial power spreading its influence. The Hebrew word, with its Aramaic-like structure, fits Ezekiel's tendency to adopt Mesopotamian loan-words during the exile period.

gloss_readable: A participial form of the common verb 'to burn,' appearing in Amos's vision of judgment where a relative comes to burn the bodies of the dead. The context is one of plague or military disaster so severe that normal burial is impossible and corpses must be cremated, a practice unusual in Israel. The burner comes to remove remains from the house in secrecy.

senses.1: The one who burns bodies during the catastrophic judgment described in Amos 6:10. In this grim scene, a kinsman enters a house to carry out the dead 'and burn them'—likely because plague or siege conditions prevented normal burial. The multilingual glosses capture the participial sense: 'his burner' or 'the one who burns him,' emphasizing the personal involvement of a relative in this tragic task.

gloss_readable: A prickly, unwanted plant contrasted with the fragrant myrtle in Isaiah's vision of restoration. When God renews the land, the worthless brier will be replaced by the noble myrtle. Ancient versions identified it as a nettle or similar noxious weed. The specific botanical identity is uncertain, but the symbolic contrast is clear: judgment's thorns versus blessing's beauty.

senses.1: The desert thorn or brier that will give way to myrtle in Isaiah 55:13, part of the prophet's vision where nature itself celebrates redemption. 'Instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle'—the transformation from cursed vegetation to fragrant beauty symbolizes the reversal of exile. The Greek and Latin versions rendered it as nettle or similar stinging plants, emphasizing its undesirable character.

gloss_readable: The name of the spy from the tribe of Asher sent by Moses to scout the land of Canaan. One of the twelve tribal representatives in Numbers 13, Sethur joined the majority report that discouraged Israel from entering the land. His name may mean 'hidden' or 'protected,' from the root meaning to conceal.

senses.1: Sethur son of Michael, the spy representing Asher in the reconnaissance of Canaan (Numbers 13:13). He was among the ten who brought back the fearful report of giants and fortified cities. The name appears in Greek transliteration as Sathour or Thasour, reflecting variations in pronunciation.

gloss_readable: A late Hebrew verb meaning to stop up or shut out, used uniquely in Lamentations where the poet laments that God has blocked his prayer from reaching heaven. The word is a variant of the more common root for 'stop up,' but here carries the sense of divine rejection. Some scholars suggest it may be related to Arabic roots meaning to frustrate or disappoint.

senses.1: The act of God shutting out prayer in Lamentations 3:8: 'He has shut out my prayer.' In the depths of Jerusalem's suffering, the speaker feels not only unheard but actively excluded—as though God has erected a barrier against supplication. The verb's rare usage and late form suggest it was chosen for its emphatic sense of blockage and refusal.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic passive participle referring to things concealed or kept secret. Daniel uses this term when praising God who 'reveals deep and hidden things' and knows what lies in darkness. The word emphasizes the contrast between divine omniscience and human limitation: what is veiled from mortals is open to God's sight.

senses.1: The hidden realities that only God can reveal, appearing in Daniel 2:22 where the prophet blesses God for disclosing Nebuchadnezzar's forgotten dream. 'He reveals the deep and hidden things'—the Aramaic emphasizes that these are not merely unknown but actively concealed, beyond the reach of human wisdom or divination. The multilingual versions consistently render this as 'hidden' or 'occult' things.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic verb meaning to destroy or demolish, cognate with Syriac and related to the Hebrew root for tearing down. In Ezra, it describes Nebuchadnezzar's destruction of Solomon's temple. The Aramaic section of Ezra uses this term to narrate the historical cause of the temple's ruin before describing its reconstruction.

senses.1: The destruction of the Jerusalem temple by Nebuchadnezzar, described in Ezra 5:12: 'he destroyed this house.' The Aramaic narrative places this verb in the mouth of the Jewish elders explaining to Tattenai why they are rebuilding: their ancestors' sins provoked God to give them into the hand of the Babylonian king, 'who destroyed this house and exiled the people.'

gloss_readable: A rare feminine noun meaning shelter or protection, used ironically in Moses' song where he mocks the false gods of Israel's enemies. 'Let them be a shelter over you,' he says sarcastically, challenging these lifeless idols to provide the safety their worshipers expect. The term normally connotes refuge, but here it drips with scorn.

senses.1: The 'shelter' that impotent pagan gods cannot provide, appearing in Deuteronomy 32:38 in Moses' satirical challenge. After describing how Israel's enemies trusted in gods who ate their sacrifices and drank their drink offerings, Moses taunts: 'Let them arise and help you, let them be your shelter!' The Hebrew construction may require emending the verb to plural (as some suggest) to match the plural subject.

gloss_readable: A Levite name from the family of Kohath, appearing in the genealogical records of Exodus. Sithri was a cousin of Moses and Aaron, descended from Uzziel. The name likely means 'my protection' or 'Yah is my shelter,' incorporating the divine name. Greek versions transliterate it variously as Seghri, Sethri, or Setri.

senses.1: Sithri son of Uzziel, a Levite listed in Exodus 6:22 among the extended family of Kohath. He represents one of the collateral lines of the priestly tribe, descended from Levi through Kohath and Uzziel. The genealogy establishes the broader clan structure within which Aaron's family held the high priesthood.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic loanword for 'works' or 'deeds,' used in Ecclesiastes' philosophical reflection on divine sovereignty and human ignorance. The plural form with Aramaic morphology appears in the context of uncertainty: 'the righteous and the wise and their works are in God's hand,' yet humans cannot know what lies ahead. This late linguistic feature marks Ecclesiastes as post-exilic.

senses.1: The deeds or works of the righteous and wise in Ecclesiastes 9:1, where the Teacher observes that despite human effort and wisdom, ultimate outcomes remain in God's hand. 'All this I laid to heart, examining it all: the righteous and the wise and their works are in God's hand'—yet whether love or hate awaits them, no one knows. The Aramaic form reflects the book's late linguistic character.

gloss_readable: A personal name meaning 'servant of El (God),' borne by a member of the Judahite nobility during Jeremiah's time. Avdeel's son Shelemiah was among the officials King Jehoiakim dispatched to arrest Jeremiah and Baruch after the reading of the prophetic scroll. Theophoric names of this type, combining 'servant' with a divine element, were common across Semitic cultures.

senses.1: Avdeel the father of Shelemiah, mentioned in Jeremiah 36:26 when King Jehoiakim commanded his son and two others to seize Jeremiah and his scribe. The name, meaning 'servant of El,' belongs to the pattern of Phoenician, Nabataean, and Sabean theophoric names that invoke deity as master or lord. Despite his son's role in persecuting Jeremiah, the Lord 'hid them.'

gloss_readable: A Gadite name meaning 'servant of El,' found in the genealogies of Transjordanian tribes. Avdiel was an ancestor of Buz, one of the chiefs of Gad. Like the similar name Avdeel, this theophoric form appears widely in Northwest Semitic inscriptions from Phoenicia, Nabatea, and South Arabia, testifying to the common practice of naming children as devotees of the high god.

senses.1: Avdiel the Gadite, listed in 1 Chronicles 5:15 within the genealogy of the tribe of Gad settled east of the Jordan. The name follows the widespread Semitic pattern of declaring the child a 'servant of God,' with parallels in Phoenician, Nabataean, and Sabean inscriptions. Greek versions transliterate it as Abdeel or Abdiel.

gloss_readable: An intensive noun denoting a crushing load of pledges or debts, appearing in Habakkuk's woe oracle against the oppressor. The prophet uses vivid language to describe the arrogant conqueror who 'loads himself with pledges' taken from victims. The Hebrew term intensifies the idea of weight and accumulation, picturing the wicked man buried under the mass of his extorted collateral.

senses.1: The heavy burden of pledges that the wicked oppressor heaps upon himself in Habakkuk 2:6. The taunt-song mocks the conqueror: 'Woe to him who loads himself with thick pledges!' The intensive form emphasizes not just debt but the oppressive, crushing weight of multiple obligations forcibly extracted. Spanish renders it as 'pledges!' with an exclamation, while French interprets it as 'stolen objects.'

gloss_readable: A Levite name appearing in the genealogical lists of 1 Chronicles, where the second occurrence may be a textual variant or distinct individual. The name is identical in form to the gentilic 'Hebrew' but functions here as a personal name. Greek manuscripts show considerable variation, transliterating it as Abai, Obdi, or Abaria.

senses.1: Ivri the Levite listed in 1 Chronicles 24:27 among the descendants of Merari in the priestly divisions. The name's identity with the word 'Hebrew' has prompted some to consider it a textual issue, though it may simply be a personal name derived from the gentilic. The variation in Greek witnesses (Abai, Obdi, Abaria) suggests early uncertainty about the reading.

gloss_terse: Evron (place name, possibly textual variant for Avdon)
gloss_readable: A town name appearing in Joshua's list of Asherite settlements, though most scholars believe the text should read 'Avdon' based on parallel passages and versions. The site is mentioned among the fortified cities of Asher's inheritance. If Evron is the original reading, the location is unknown; if a scribal error for Avdon, it refers to a Levitical city in the same region.

senses.1: Evron, listed among the towns of Asher in Joshua 19:28, though textual evidence suggests reading 'Avdon' instead. The Greek versions render it Elbon, Achran, or similar forms, showing early uncertainty. BDB notes the site is 'probably' to be read as Avdon, a Levitical city elsewhere assigned to Asher, making this potentially a scribal variant of that better-known name.

gloss_readable: A verb describing the shriveling of grain seeds in Joel's agricultural disaster. The prophet uses this rare word to depict the complete crop failure accompanying the locust plague: 'the grains have shriveled under their clods.' Related to Arabic words for contracting or frowning, the Hebrew emphasizes the withering and collapse of what should have been full, viable seed.

senses.1: The shriveling of seed grains under drought conditions in Joel 1:17, part of the prophet's description of agricultural catastrophe. 'The grains shrivel beneath the clods, the storehouses are desolate, the barns are broken down'—the verb vividly pictures dried-up kernels that never sprouted, contracting and collapsing in the parched soil. The root's connection to Arabic 'contract' or 'frown' captures the image of curling inward.

gloss_readable: A verb meaning to weave or wind together, used metaphorically in Micah for the intricate plotting of corrupt leaders. The prophet describes how 'the prince asks, the judge is ready for a bribe, and the great man utters his evil desire—thus they weave it together.' The image is of skilled conspirators intertwining their schemes like threads in a fabric.

senses.1: The weaving together of corrupt schemes in Micah 7:3, where officials collaborate to pervert justice. 'The prince asks, the judge accepts bribes, the powerful dictate what they desire—and together they weave it.' The verb pictures conspiracy as skilled craftsmanship, the careful intertwining of multiple strands of corruption into a unified web. Some propose emending to a root meaning 'twist' or 'pervert,' but the weaving metaphor fits Micah's artistry.

gloss_readable: A feminine noun denoting lustful craving or inordinate passion, used in Ezekiel's allegory of Jerusalem's adultery. The prophet describes personified Jerusalem as exceeding even her 'sister' Samaria in her lustfulness and harlotry. The word is parallel to 'fornications,' emphasizing the intensity and perversity of Judah's idolatry portrayed as sexual unfaithfulness.

senses.1: The lustful passion of personified Jerusalem in Ezekiel 23:11, where the prophet accuses Judah of surpassing Samaria in spiritual adultery. 'She became more corrupt than her sister in her lust and in her harlotries'—the Hebrew term emphasizes intense, degrading craving. The parallel with 'harlotries' reinforces the image of covenant unfaithfulness as compulsive sexual betrayal.

gloss_readable: A verb expressing deep grief or anguish for another's suffering, appearing in Job's self-defense. Job asks rhetorically, 'Did I not weep for the one whose day was hard? Was not my soul grieved for the poor?' The word conveys sympathetic suffering, the inner anguish one feels witnessing another's misery. Cognates in Aramaic and possibly Akkadian carry similar emotional intensity.

senses.1: Job's grief for the suffering poor in Job 30:25, where he protests his innocence by recalling his compassion. 'Did I not weep for the one in trouble? Was not my soul grieved for the needy?'—the verb emphasizes inner anguish, not mere pity but soul-level suffering with those in distress. The parallel with 'weep' shows this is more than intellectual sympathy; it is emotional participation in another's pain.

gloss_terse: shut oneself off (from marriage), remain unmarried
gloss_readable: A Niphal verb meaning to shut or confine oneself, used in Ruth for voluntary abstention from marriage. Naomi asks her daughters-in-law whether they would 'shut themselves off from belonging to a man' while waiting for her infant sons to grow up. The image is of self-imposed isolation or confinement, withdrawing from normal life. Later rabbinic Hebrew uses related forms for refraining from marriage.

senses.1: The self-imposed seclusion from marriage in Ruth 1:13, where Naomi rhetorically asks whether Ruth and Orpah would 'shut yourselves off so as not to belong to a man.' The verb pictures voluntary confinement or withdrawal—restraining oneself from marriage while waiting indefinitely. The context shows the absurdity of Naomi's situation: even if she bore sons tonight, would these young women seclude themselves until the boys matured?

gloss_readable: A plural noun denoting menstruation or the menstrual period, used metaphorically in Isaiah for ritual impurity. The prophet compares Israel's best deeds to 'a garment of menstruation'—stained, unclean, utterly defiled. The image is deliberately repulsive, emphasizing that even the nation's righteousness is contaminated by sin. The word evokes the ceremonial uncleanness associated with menstrual flow in Levitical law.

senses.1: The menstrual stain metaphor in Isaiah 64:6, where the prophet confesses, 'All our righteous deeds are like a garment of menstruation.' The image shocks: what Israel considers good works are, before God's holiness, as unclean as a cloth stained with menstrual blood. The plural form may intensify the sense of defilement. The parallel with 'we all are unclean' shows this is about pervasive ritual and moral pollution.

gloss_readable: A feminine adjective meaning voluptuous or pleasure-seeking, used as a noun to personify Babylon in Isaiah's taunt. The prophet addresses Babylon as 'O voluptuous one, dwelling securely,' mocking her self-indulgent confidence before announcing her sudden downfall. The term evokes luxury, sensuality, and false security.

senses.1: Babylon personified as a voluptuous woman in Isaiah 47:8, addressed in the prophet's taunt oracle. 'Now hear this, O voluptuous one, who sits securely'—the feminine adjective becomes a mocking title, emphasizing Babylon's self-indulgent complacency. The context contrasts her luxurious ease with the humiliation about to come: stripped, exposed, bereaved, enslaved.

gloss_readable: The name of a Reubenite warrior, one of David's mighty men according to 1 Chronicles. Adina son of Shiza was a chief of the Reubenites with thirty men under his command. The name likely derives from the root meaning 'delicate' or 'refined,' ironic for a battle-hardened captain. Greek versions render it as Adina or Adeina.

senses.1: Adina son of Shiza the Reubenite, listed in 1 Chronicles 11:42 among David's elite warriors. He was not only one of the mighty men but also a leader over thirty Reubenites. The name, meaning something like 'delicate' or 'refined,' provides an interesting contrast to his military role—perhaps bestowed in childhood or reflecting a family heritage.

gloss_readable: A name appearing in 2 Samuel's list of David's mighty men, though most scholars believe the text is corrupt and should be read differently based on the parallel in 1 Chronicles. The phrase 'Adino the Eznite' likely represents a scribal error for 'he wielded his spear,' as suggested by the Chronicles parallel. If original, the name would derive from the root for 'delicate' or 'voluptuous.'

senses.1: The problematic 'Adino' in 2 Samuel 23:8, where the text reads 'Adino the Eznite' but parallel passages suggest corruption. BDB and most commentators recommend reading 'he wielded his spear' based on 1 Chronicles 11:11, which clarifies the original sense: the warrior lifted his spear against eight hundred slain at one time. The Greek and other versions show early confusion, supporting the textual emendation.

gloss_readable: A town in the Shephelah lowlands of Judah, listed among the settlements in Joshua's territorial allotment. The name appears to be a dual form, possibly meaning 'two Aditas' or indicating a twin settlement. The precise location is unknown. Greek manuscripts offer variant transliterations, reflecting uncertainty about the name's pronunciation and meaning.

senses.1: Aditayim, a town assigned to Judah in Joshua 15:36 within the Shephelah district. The dual ending suggests either a double settlement or a place name with dual morphology for unclear reasons. Greek versions render it Adiathaeim, Ageththaim, or similar forms. The site has not been identified with any modern location.

gloss_readable: A personal name borne by the father of one of David's officers. Shaphat son of Adlai was overseer of David's herds in the valleys. The name may mean 'justice of Yah' or 'my justice,' incorporating a theophoric element, though the etymology is uncertain. Greek versions transliterate it as Adai or Adli.

senses.1: Adlai the father of Shaphat, mentioned in 1 Chronicles 27:29 among David's administrative officials. Shaphat son of Adlai supervised the royal herds that grazed in the valleys. The name likely contains a divine element, possibly meaning 'my justice' or 'Yah's justice,' though its exact derivation remains unclear.

gloss_readable: A Hitpael verb meaning to luxuriate or take exquisite pleasure in something, used in Nehemiah's confession to describe Israel's indulgence in God's goodness during the conquest era. The people 'ate, were filled, grew fat, and luxuriated in your great goodness.' The verb implies sensory delight and self-indulgent pleasure, here directed toward God's abundant provision.

senses.1: Israel's luxuriating in divine bounty during the conquest, described in Nehemiah 9:25. After listing the good things Israel received—fortified cities, fertile land, cisterns, vineyards, olive groves—Nehemiah says, 'they ate, were satisfied, grew fat, and luxuriated in your great goodness.' The verb climaxes the sequence, picturing Israel delighting themselves in lavish abundance before the eventual rebellion.

gloss_terse: Adadah (place name, possibly textual corruption for Aroer)
gloss_readable: A place name in southern Judah's town list, though some scholars propose reading 'Aroer' instead based on other geographical references. If original, Adadah is otherwise unknown. The site appears in Joshua's allocation to Judah among the southernmost settlements toward the Edomite border. The name's similarity to other variants has led to ongoing debate about the correct reading.

senses.1: Adadah listed among the towns of southern Judah in Joshua 15:22, though textual critics suggest emending to 'Aroer' (or 'Ararah') based on the Septuagint and parallel town lists. BDB notes that the form may be a corruption of the better-known Aroer in southern Judah mentioned in 1 Samuel 30:28. The uncertainty reflects the challenges of reconstructing ancient toponymy from variant manuscript traditions.

gloss_terse: help, assist (Aramaic loanword, possible textual variant)
gloss_readable: An Aramaic loanword meaning to help, appearing in a textually uncertain passage of 1 Chronicles. The phrase 'to help' in 12:34 likely represents a scribal variant for the more common Hebrew root meaning 'to arrange' or 'set in order,' used elsewhere in the chapter for arranging battle lines. Syriac and rabbinic sources use this Aramaic root as equivalent to Hebrew 'to help.'

senses.1: The infinitive 'to help' in 1 Chronicles 12:34 (or v. 33 in some versifications), though many scholars emend to 'to arrange [for battle]' based on parallel verses and context. If the Aramaic reading is original, it means 'to assist' or 'help,' borrowed from Syriac/Targumic usage. The phrase describes warriors who came 'to help' or 'to array for battle,' with Greek and other versions supporting the emendation to the common root for military formation.

gloss_readable: A Benjamite personal name meaning 'flock' or 'herd,' appearing in the genealogical records of 1 Chronicles. Eder was one of the sons listed in the family of Benjamin. The name uses a common noun for a herd of animals as a personal designation, possibly reflecting pastoral heritage. Greek versions offer various transliterations.

senses.1: Eder the Benjamite listed in 1 Chronicles 8:15 among the genealogies of Benjamin. The name, identical to the common word for 'flock,' may reflect the family's pastoral background or simply a naming tradition using animal husbandry terms. Greek manuscripts transliterate it as Oded, Oder, or Adar.

gloss_readable: A town in the far south of Judah, listed among the settlements toward the Edomite border. Eder appears in Joshua's catalogue of Judahite towns but its precise location is unknown. The name means 'flock' or 'herd,' perhaps indicating a pastoral settlement or watering place for livestock. Greek versions show considerable variation in transliteration.

senses.1: The town of Eder in extreme southern Judah, mentioned in Joshua 15:21 near the border with Edom. The name, meaning 'flock,' may suggest a grazing area or shepherding settlement. The site has not been identified with certainty. Greek versions render it as Ara, Edrai, or Eber, showing early uncertainty about the vocalization.

gloss_terse: becloud, cover with a cloud (divine judgment metaphor)
gloss_readable: A Hiphil verb meaning to cover with a cloud or enshroud in darkness, used in Lamentations for God's judgment on Jerusalem. The prophet laments, 'How the Lord has clouded Daughter Zion in his anger!' The image is of divine wrath descending like a storm cloud, darkening and obscuring what was once glorious. The verb intensifies the sense of God's alienation and judgment.

senses.1: The divine clouding of Jerusalem in judgment, expressed in Lamentations 2:1: 'How the Lord has beclouded Daughter Zion in his anger!' The verb pictures God's wrath as a dark cloud covering the city, hiding her glory and beauty. The cloud imagery suggests both divine presence (as at Sinai) now turned hostile, and the darkness of disaster obscuring former splendor.

gloss_readable: A descendant of Joktan listed in the Table of Nations, representing an Arabian people group. Obal appears in Genesis 10 among the sons of Joktan, the ancestor of various South Arabian tribes. The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles calls him Ebal, showing the interchange of 'o' and 'e' vowels in variant traditions. The specific location or people remains uncertain.

senses.1: Obal, a descendant of Joktan in Genesis 10:28, representing one of the Joktanite Arabian tribes. The name also appears as Ebal in 1 Chronicles 1:22, reflecting variant vowel traditions. Early geographers attempted to locate Obal's descendants in South Arabia, but precise identification remains elusive. The name situates this group among the Arabian peoples tracing ancestry to Shem through Eber and Joktan.

gloss_terse: bake (a bread-cake), make into a round loaf
gloss_readable: A denominative verb meaning to bake a cake or form bread into a round loaf, appearing in Ezekiel's symbolic action. God commands the prophet to bake barley cakes over a fire fueled by human dung, symbolizing the defiled food Israel will eat in exile. The verb derives from the noun for a round bread-cake, emphasizing the shaping and baking process.

senses.1: The baking of bread-cakes in Ezekiel 4:12, where God commands the prophet to perform a sign-act of coming exile: 'You shall bake it as a barley cake, and you shall bake it on human dung in their sight.' The verb, derived from the noun for 'round cake,' emphasizes the forming and cooking of the bread into its characteristic shape—here made ritually unclean to symbolize the defilement of exile.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic adverb meaning 'still' or 'yet,' indicating ongoing action or state. In Daniel, it describes how Nebuchadnezzar's boastful words were still in his mouth when divine judgment fell. The adverb emphasizes the immediacy of God's response: even before the king finished speaking, the sentence was executed. The word is common in biblical Aramaic and rabbinic literature.

senses.1: The immediacy marker 'still' in Daniel 4:31, where the text says, 'While the word was still in the king's mouth, a voice fell from heaven.' Nebuchadnezzar was boasting about his achievements when, mid-sentence, divine judgment struck. The Aramaic adverb emphasizes the overlap: his prideful words were not yet complete when God's response came, underscoring the swiftness of divine retribution.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic plural noun meaning iniquities or sins, appearing with a pronominal suffix in Daniel. The word occurs in Daniel's interpretation when he urges Nebuchadnezzar to 'break off your iniquities by righteousness.' The Aramaic form corresponds to the Hebrew root for 'perversity' or 'iniquity,' referring to moral crookedness and rebellion against God.

senses.1: Nebuchadnezzar's iniquities in Daniel 4:27, where Daniel counsels the king: 'Break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed.' The Aramaic plural with suffix ('your iniquities') parallels 'your sins' in the previous clause, emphasizing the accumulated moral guilt that demands repentance. Daniel offers a path to avert judgment through justice and compassion.

gloss_readable: A masculine noun denoting an unjust or wicked person, appearing in Job's complaint. Job laments that God has handed him over to 'the unjust' or 'the wicked one.' The term emphasizes moral perversity and injustice rather than general sinfulness. It may refer to specific enemies or use the singular collectively for the wicked as a class.

senses.1: The unjust person or wicked one to whom Job feels delivered in Job 16:11: 'God has delivered me to the unjust and cast me into the hands of the wicked.' The noun emphasizes moral crookedness and injustice—Job perceives himself as handed over to those who pervert righteousness. The term may be singular representing a class or refer to specific adversaries Job sees as agents of his suffering.

gloss_readable: A personal name appearing among those who married foreign wives during the post-exilic period. Olam is listed in Ezra 10 among the Israelites who had intermarried and were called to separate. The name is identical to the common word meaning 'eternity' or 'long duration,' though here it functions as a personal designation. The context is the religious reform under Ezra.

senses.1: Olam, one of the Israelites who had married foreign women according to Ezra 10:2 (following the context). The name, identical to the word for 'eternity' or 'everlasting,' was apparently used as a personal name in the post-exilic community. He was among those identified during Ezra's reform requiring separation from foreign wives to preserve covenant purity.

gloss_readable: A denominative verb from 'eye,' meaning to look at someone with envy or suspicion. The word appears in 1 Samuel describing Saul's attitude toward David after the women's song praising David's victories. 'Saul eyed David from that day forward'—a continuous, jealous watching. The verb captures the idea of keeping a suspicious, envious eye on someone perceived as a rival.

senses.1: Saul's jealous watching of David in 1 Samuel 18:9, after hearing the women sing, 'Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.' The text says Saul 'eyed David from that day onward'—the denominative verb pictures the king's suspicious, envious gaze fixed on his rival. The Qere/Ketiv variation shows textual uncertainty, but all traditions preserve the sense of hostile scrutiny driven by jealousy.
